definition: In computer science, computational intelligence (CI) refers to concepts, paradigms, algorithms and implementations of systems that are designed to show "intelligent" behavior in complex and changing environments.
details: These systems are aimed at mastering complex tasks in a wide variety of technical or commercial areas and offer solutions that recognize and interpret patterns, control processes, support decision-making or autonomously manoeuvre vehicles or robots in unknown environments, among other things. These concepts and paradigms are characterized by the ability to learn or adapt to new situations, to generalize, to abstract, to discover and associate. Nature-analog or nature-inspired methods play a key role in this. CI approaches primarily address those complex real-world problems for which traditional or mathematical modeling is not appropriate for various reasons: the processes cannot be described exactly with complete knowledge, the processes are too complex for mathematical reasoning, they contain some uncertainties during the process, such as unforeseen changes in the environment or in the process itself, or the processes are simply stochastic in nature. Thus, CI techniques are properly aimed at processes that are ill-defined, complex, nonlinear, time-varying and/or stochastic. A recent definition of the IEEE Computational Intelligence Societey describes CI as the theory, design, application and development of biologically and linguistically motivated computational paradigms. Traditionally the three main pillars of CI have been Neural Networks, Fuzzy Systems and Evolutionary Computation. ... CI is an evolving field and at present in addition to the three main constituents, it encompasses computing paradigms like ambient intelligence, artificial life, cultural learning, artificial endocrine networks, social reasoning, and artificial hormone networks. ... Over the last few years there has been an explosion of research on Deep Learning, in particular deep convolutional neural networks. Nowadays, deep learning has become the core method for artificial intelligence. In fact, some of the most successful AI systems are based on CI. However, as CI is an emerging and developing field there is no final definition of CI, especially in terms of the list of concepts and paradigms that belong to it. The general requirements for the development of an “intelligent system” are ultimately always the same, namely the simulation of intelligent thinking and action in a specific area of application. To do this, the knowledge about this area must be represented in a model so that it can be processed. The quality of the resulting system depends largely on how well the model was chosen in the development process. Sometimes data-driven methods are suitable for finding a good model and sometimes logic-based knowledge representations deliver better results. Hybrid models are usually used in real applications. According to actual textbooks, the following methods and paradigms, which largely complement each other, can be regarded as parts of CI: Fuzzy systems Neural networks and, in particular, convolutional neural networks Evolutionary computation and, in particular, multi-objective evolutionary optimization Swarm intelligence Bayesian networks Artificial immune systems Learning theory Probabilistic methods

explainer.lead: Computational intelligence is a collection of ways to build systems that learn and adapt when a neat mathematical description of the problem is out of reach. It matters because many practical tasks, from recognizing patterns to steering robots, involve uncertainty, change and complexity. Its traditional building blocks are neural networks, fuzzy systems and evolutionary computation, often combined with other approaches.

tiers.eli5: Imagine teaching a robot to find its way through a house where the furniture keeps moving. Instead of writing a perfect rule for every possible room, you give it ways to learn from experience, work with rough clues such as “quite close,” and improve by trying different variations. Computational intelligence is the name for this toolbox of learning and adapting methods.
tiers.practitioner: CI is useful for ill-defined, nonlinear, time-varying or stochastic processes where an exact mathematical model is unavailable or impractical. Typical building blocks include neural and convolutional networks, fuzzy systems, evolutionary and multi-objective optimization, swarm intelligence, Bayesian networks and probabilistic methods. Model choice strongly affects system quality, real applications often use hybrids, and unforeseen changes or uncertainty in the process remain important pitfalls.
tiers.paperLevel: Consider a task whose underlying process cannot be described exactly with complete knowledge, is too complex for mathematical reasoning, contains uncertainty, or is stochastic. CI studies the theory, design, application and development of biologically and linguistically motivated computational paradigms that learn, adapt, generalize, abstract, discover and associate to produce intelligent behavior. Neural networks, fuzzy systems and evolutionary computation are its traditional pillars, but the field’s boundaries remain unsettled. The resulting system depends heavily on how well its application model was chosen, with data-driven, logic-based and hybrid representations all possible.

explainer.example: A delivery robot entering an unfamiliar warehouse could use a neural network to recognize obstacles, fuzzy rules to turn rough distance judgments into steering decisions, and evolutionary computation to improve those rules. When the layout changes, the system can adapt instead of relying on an exact mathematical description of every aisle.

usedIn.name: Autonomous vehicles and robots
usedIn.detail: Helping vehicles and robots manoeuvre autonomously in unknown environments.

explainer.intuition: Some problems are too messy, changeable or uncertain for a complete hand-built mathematical model. CI approaches instead provide ways to learn, adapt and generalize, often drawing inspiration from biological or linguistic processes.
howItWorks: Start with a complex task, its goals and observations of the process or environment.
Choose one or more CI paradigms, such as neural networks, fuzzy systems or evolutionary computation.
Represent knowledge about the application in a model that a computer can process.
Use learning, adaptation, search or probabilistic reasoning to develop or improve that model.
Apply the model to recognize patterns, control a process, support decisions or guide autonomous action.
explainer.whyItMatters: CI offers practical ways to tackle processes that are ill-defined, complex, nonlinear, time-varying or stochastic. It complements rather than eliminates careful modeling: the quality of the chosen model remains crucial, and real applications often combine data-driven and logic-based methods.
misconceptions: CI is not simply another name for all artificial intelligence; it is an evolving field with no final list of included paradigms.
CI is not limited to neural networks or deep learning; fuzzy systems and evolutionary computation are also traditional pillars.
Using CI does not remove the need for a suitable model, and no single paradigm is best for every application.
